yasminsati bhavatyeva yattato'nyasya kalpane | taddhetutvena sarvatra hetūnāmanavasthitiḥ || ityādi || 6 || evaṃ dharmī eva tāvadātmā nāstīti kutra hetūpanyāsairaiśvaryaṃ prasādhyeteti uktvā jñānakriyāyogāditi yo heturuktaḥ, tat nirākartuṃ jñānameva parasya na upapannaṃ jaḍatvena ajaḍatvena veti parasya prasaṅgāpādanaṃ kartuṃ kārikādvayaṃ prasaṅgaviparyayeṇa svamatalābho yataḥ | tathāhi yayā yuktyā ātmā nityaḥ, tayā jñānamapi nityaṃ kasmāt | nityatve tasya taditi katham | tato dharmihetusvarūpayoranyonyarūpavirodhena āśrayāśrayibhāvavirodhena ca siddhiriti | tatra prathamamajaḍarūpatve jñānaṃ siddhāntino na upapadyate iti yat sūtreṇa ucyate, tat saṃkṣepeṇa avatārayati ātmanaḥ iti | sūtre anityam iti prādhānyādupāttaṃ dharmāntarāṇyapi vailakṣaṇyakārīṇi upalakṣayatītyāśayena dvitvavikalpeneti sāmānyena āha | ātmāpi citsvabhāvo jñānamapi, tato dvitvena anyatvena nityatvānityatvalakṣaṇena dharmadharmibhāvena ca yā kalpanā kṛtā, sā anupapannā, pramāṇamūlatvābhāvāt na vastusādhanītyetadvastu āha jñānaṃ ca citsvarūpaṃ cettadanityaṃ kimātmavat | athāpi jaḍametasya kathamarthaprakāśatā || 7 || cakāraḥ siddhāntinaṃ prati anupapattyantaraṃ samuccinoti | jñānasya yadi cidrūpatā ātmana iva svābhāvikī, tarhi tat kimanityam | naiva anityamātmavadeva | citsvabhāvatvasya svaprakāśatvalakṣaṇasya hi viruddhaṃ vedyarūpatvaṃ paraprakāśyatārūpaṃ svātantryapāratantryayorvirodhāt, vedyatvena ca vyāpto deśakālayoga iti vyāpakaviruddhasya svaprakāśatvasya upalabdhyā jñāne (page 134) viruddhavyāptasya deśakālayogasya niṣedhaḥ | deśakālayoga eva ca anityatvam | niyataṃ hi yat bhavati, natu na bhavati kathaṃcit; tat nityam | yacca kvacit bhavati, kadācicca bhavati; tadanyatra anyadā ca na bhavatyapīti na niyataṃbhavam | sakaladeśakālayoge'pi vastutastadayoga eva | yadi hi tena deśena, tena vā kālena na asya svarūpamāviśyate, tat tatreti tadeti vā kutaḥ | āvṛta iti cet, tena ya ā samantāt vṛtaḥ, tasya kathamanyena dhāraṇam | vṛtto hi avaṣṭ
**The cognition cannot be a thing: the dilemma of the consciousness-form** The Buddhist had denied the self. But he had also, in a different mood, offered a reason for the self's lordship — "by the union of knowledge and action." To stop even this, Abhinavagupta turns the same logic against the cognition itself. Whatever the opponent says cognition is, it cannot stand. And he forces the choice with a single dilemma, put in the seventh kārikā: if the cognition is of the consciousness-form, then it must be eternal, like the self; but if it is inert, then it cannot reveal any object at all. There is no third option. Take the first horn. The consciousness-nature is, by its very marker, *self-manifestation* — it is the light that knows itself. And self-manifestation is directly opposed to being-an-object, to being manifested by another. A thing that is manifest by another is caught in place and time — it is here or there, now or then. But the self-manifest light is free of all such being-caught. If the cognition were truly of the consciousness-form, it could not be the momentary, place-and-time-bound thing the Buddhist takes it to be; it would have to be eternal and omnipresent, exactly like the self. And then the Buddhist's whole picture — a stream of fleeting cognitions, each a separate momentary quality — falls apart. The cognition would not be a momentary flash; it would be the eternal light itself. The Buddhist tries to escape by saying: "the cognition is not the self's own form; it is a quality of the self, made by the union with the mind." But this, Abhinavagupta shows, fails too. For what we call the cognition is the manifestation of the blue and the rest; and if that manifestation is only an occasional quality, absent when its cause is absent, then the self, apart from it, is simply not manifesting the blue. The cognition, taken as a separate thing, has no place to stand. Whether you call it consciousness-form or a quality, it dissolves. The second horn is no better. If the cognition is inert — a dead thing, like the objects — then how could it reveal anything? An inert thing does not shine; it is shone upon. It cannot be the manifestation of the blue, for manifestation is not a property of the inert. So the inert cognition cannot account for the one thing it is supposed to explain — the appearing of objects. And beneath both horns lies a deeper point. If the cognition were a separate thing, caught in place and time, it would have to be held and supported by something; but the self-manifest light cannot be held or covered by another — the covered thing, we might say, could not bear another's support. So the whole idea of a cognition as an object supported by a self collapses, and with it the Buddhist's reason for the self's lordship. What survives the collapse is the light itself. The cognition is not a thing to be placed and timed; it is the self-manifestation, which is the self. And this is what leads Abhinavagupta to the Sāṃkhya's buddhi — the intellect — which the Sāṃkhya makes the locus of the cognitions. For even there, the same dilemma will hold: if the buddhi is consciousness-form it is eternal, if inert it cannot manifest. The cognition is not a quality to be located anywhere; it is the self-manifest light, which is the self — and the union of knowledge and action, far from being a reason for lordship that the opponent can offer, is simply the self's own nature, the knowing and the acting of the one light. ---

> The kārikā: knowledge is of the nature of consciousness (jñānaṃ citsvarūpam). Against the > Vaiśeṣika/Nyāya view that knowledge is a quality produced in the self by its contact with an object, > Abhinavagupta holds that knowledge is consciousness-natured — it is self-luminous, manifesting both > the object and itself. This is the root of the two claims that follow: the cognition cannot be > reduced to an inert quality (V1-G), and it is ultimately self-cognition (V1-K). The kārikā states the > positive essence from which the refutations proceed. Vaiśeṣika/Nyāya view rejected.
